catalog_quote: stress generally falls on the second to the last syllable of the underlying root. Thus, the accented syllable remains fixed on the second to the last syllable of the root, regardless of the addition of prefixes or suffixes.
sweep_summary: All three works with stress in the title are one work: Carol Laidig's 'Segments, Syllables, and Stress in Larike' (UTA MA thesis 1990; published as SIL/UTA Publications in Linguistics 108, pp. 67-126, 1992; Glottolog 675330 is a duplicate record of the 1992 chapter). It is squarely about Larike word stress and is the primary analysis behind the StressTyp2/Gordon 2002 codings, but no open copy exists: HathiTrust holds three search-only copies (record 002583010), archive.org/Open Library/ERIC have nothing, and sil. Acquisition priority: high for the 1992 chapter (Harvard print copy; a library scan), medium for the thesis. What was read first-hand: the two held Laidig & Laidig statements — the 1995 NUSA 38 synopsis sec. 2.6 (p.23: stress 'always associated with the underlying penultimate syllable of the root, stress does not shift with affixation', epenthetic vowels extrametrical, contraction rule) and the 1991 grammar p.26 (the catalog's quote, re-verified at PDF p.40). Both confirm the catalog's fixed-strict coding; the only refinement on offer is second-hand via the local StressTyp2 dump, which attributes to Laidig 1992 an alternating secondary-stress pattern and a closed set of finally/antepenultimately stressed lexical exceptions ([maˈsa], [kudaˈpa], [siˈnorai], [ˈniriə]) — worth carrying as a note, not a reclassification, until the 1992 chapter is read. No new deciding source; the 1995 sec. 2.6 quotation is the sharper of the two held statements and could replace the 1991 'generally falls' sentence as the displayed quote.

new_statements.quote: To assign word stress in Larike, it is necessary to have access to the underlying root. The general stress rule is that stress is always associated with the underlying penultimate syllable of the root, stress does not shift with affixation. It should be emphasized that the underlying penultimate syllable is not always the same as the surface penultimate syllable. For example, there are several roots that contain a final VV sequence, such as [pa'tae] 'to leave' where the VV sequence is pronounced as a surface diphthong. Therefore, [pa'tae] is realized on the surface as a two-syllable word, apparently receiving stress on the ultimate syllable.

new_statements.reading: Primary stress is fixed on the penultimate syllable of the underlying ROOT and does not move under prefixation or suffixation (ana-na [ˈʔanana] vs anana [ʔaˈnana]; pa-kadi-ku [paˈkadiku] vs paka-diku [pakaˈdiku], ex. 9 p.23); epenthetic -u/-e are extrametrical (iʔan-u [ˈʔiʔanu], ator-e [ˈʔatore], exx. 10-11 p.23-24); in contractions stress falls on 'the surface syllable containing the underlying, penultimate syllable of the right-most root' (p.24). Apparent minimal pairs are morphological, so stress is not lexically contrastive. This confirms the catalog's fixed-strict coding, with the domain being the root, not the surface word — surface stress is antepenultimate or earlier under suffixation and final when a root ends in VV. Same authors and same statement as the 1991 grammar sentence the catalog quotes (Laidig & Laidig 1991:26 = PDF p.40 of, re-verified this search of works with stress in the title: 'stress generally falls on the second to the last syllable of the underlying root.. regardless of the addition of prefixes or suffixes'), but more explicit about rule, domain, extrametricality and examples. It defers the exceptions to C. Laidig 1992, which remains unread.

sources.quote: "Understanding stress placement in Larike words in not entirely straightforward. For the purposes of this desc[r]iption, however, it will suffice to simply state the dominant stress pattern: stress generally falls on the second to the last syllable of the underlying root. Thus, the accented syllable remains fixed on the second to the last syllable of the root, regardless of the addition of prefixes or suffixes."
